stories.title: a room is a place
stories.moment: Callum sent me a paragraph about why the old scheduler felt wrong. "A room is a place and an appointment is a promise and we were treating both as boxes," he wrote. A place is persistent, it has a location. A promise is conditional and belongs to people, not to a grid. So the room should be a column that exists whether anything is scheduled or not. I wrote back: "this is the smartest thing anyone has said about this product." He sent conflict states the next day.
stories.why_it_matters: The entire visual logic changed because someone named the difference out loud.

stories.title: invoice sitting in approvals
stories.moment: Callum sent his invoice to Dane's email on April 20th. I redirected him to accounting. He asked about it again May 8th. I didn't answer for thirteen days, then discovered the PO number was wrong and asked him to resend. He pointed out he'd just copied it from last month. Four days later I admitted Dane had changed the format in QuickBooks without telling anyone. On June 16th he wrote that rent was tomorrow and he was short. Dane had left it sitting in approvals, not realizing it needed two signatures now. I pushed it through.
stories.why_it_matters: He had to ask three times over eight weeks for money he'd already earned.

stories.title: k
stories.moment: Every design revision ends the same way. I say "yes that" or "this is right" or send a thumbs-up emoji. He writes back "k" and moves to the next thing. The icon decision in April: "k." The solid fills in May: "k." The room block, the conflict states, the thumbnails, the placeholder text. No acknowledgment, no explanation of what he'll do next, just the single letter. Then a Figma link appears, sometimes the same day, sometimes a week later, with the thing already done.
stories.why_it_matters: The shortest possible reply became the most reliable signal that he'd heard me.

forgotten.summary: Callum asked what the scheduling view should say when there's no appointments yet. I said 'good question' but never actually provided an answer, so he used placeholder text.
forgotten.suggested_action: Send Callum the actual copy I want for the empty state on the scheduling view.

prep.last_substantive_interaction: He delivered final design handoff on June 27 before scaling back his hours, and I confirmed it was good.

stories.title: Westbrook migrated without telling anyone
stories.moment: Dane checked the database and found that Westbrook had logged in after a week of silence and moved all their historical records into the system. They didn't announce it, didn't ask for help, just did it. He sent three messages in a row trying to figure out what it meant and whether we should call them. I told him to wait a week and see if they actually used it. Four days after that, he wrote back: "you were right about the runway thing I just didn't want to hear it in may." The concession arrived by email, in the middle of a thread about scoping billing down.
stories.why_it_matters: The customer action that mattered most happened in total silence.

stories.title: He bought the booth before asking
stories.moment: Dane sent me three messages about a $2400 conference booth next to the Purina stand at the VMX summit in August. He explained why it was perfect, said basically every clinic owner in the northwest would be there, then admitted he'd already told them we'd take it. The third message was just the word "sorry." I wrote back "ok" and nothing else. Two weeks later he floated a rule for whether we'd actually staff it: go if Westbrook converts before the 15th, skip it if they don't. I agreed. Neither of us mentioned that he'd already committed the money.
stories.why_it_matters: The apology came after the commitment, and the condition came after the apology.

stories.title: He asked about Nkechi three times
stories.moment: On June 9th, Dane asked if we'd heard back from Nkechi and said we needed to look at other people if she wasn't moving. I said I'd ping her that week. Thirteen days later he asked again, then clarified that the billing plan changed a lot depending on whether it was me and Callum or me and an actual engineer. I wrote back "still talking to her" and nothing else. He did not ask again. The gap between his second ask and my answer was thirteen days. The thing he wanted to know was whether we were hiring her. The thing I told him was that a conversation was ongoing.
stories.why_it_matters: The question was binary and the answer was a continuous present tense.

stories.title: Failure stories are more useful than success stories
stories.moment: Marguerite signed the investment documents on April 6th and immediately asked to be added to updates. Then she offered to introduce me to two people who had tried to sell into veterinary practices and failed at it. I wrote back that this was "the single most useful offer anyone has made me this year," which I meant, because I'd been collecting advice from people who succeeded and learning almost nothing. She sent the introductions a week later: Corbin Achebe, who built scheduling software for equine practices and shut it down after eighteen months, and Lena Orosco, who spent two years failing to sell into dental offices. Both had actually done the thing I was trying to do, in adjacent markets, and quit.

stories.title: I did not answer the third question

I answered the first two in detail the next day: the rewrite took eleven days, Rosalind at Cascade was using the system daily, the other two pilots had gone quiet. Then I sent the May monthly update on the 31st. She replied the same day, said it was the right level of detail, and that she'd have questions next week. On June 8th she wrote back: "I do not think you answered the third question." She was right. The question had been whether anyone was paying me yet, and I had written around it for two weeks. I admitted this on June 10th and said nobody was paying, that I'd been reluctant to ask Rosalind for money while the product was still breaking, and that I wanted to take her a paid plan in July.

She wrote after our phone call to say she'd been gentler on the phone than she actually felt, and that she couldn't have her techs working around my software. I spent the weekend rebuilding the scheduler so rooms could be reserved directly, with no appointment attached. When I told her it would take two weeks, she wrote back that the timeline was what told her it was the right answer.

stories.title: Water in the rear bathroom was never water
stories.moment: Ezra sent a three-point inspection report explaining that standing water in the bathroom was not a plumbing issue but a drainage characteristic of the building's original construction. He returned the next morning and confirmed the water level had decreased, which he said proved his assessment correct. The day after that he sent a final note: the floor was dry, and if water appeared again it would resolve naturally within twenty-four to forty-eight hours. I sent one reply across all three emails, long.
stories.why_it_matters: The conclusion arrived before any of the evidence did.

stories.title: We were washing our hands too hard
stories.moment: Water appeared again five weeks later. This time Ezra wrote that he was observing excessive water usage at the sinks, improper paper towel disposal, and floor mats not being used as intended. I asked whether the floor was flooding because we were washing our hands too enthusiastically. He clarified the next day: not flooding, water accumulation due to usage patterns, and the distinction mattered from a liability perspective. The faucet pressure was commercial-grade and the basin was shallow, so water exited the perimeter when used without attention to splashing. I wrote back that we would be more careful.
stories.why_it_matters: The problem changed shape the second time it appeared.

stories.title: Confirmed, for the record
stories.moment: After an incident he did not describe, Ezra sent a five-point outline of tenant responsibilities for shared facilities. I replied: acknowledged. He wrote back the next day to say he would need explicit confirmation that we agreed to observe points one through five, and that a simple 'agreed' or 'confirmed' would suffice. I sent the word confirmed. He filed it and said that if future incidents occurred, he would refer back to the exchange and to the responsibilities as outlined on June 15.
stories.why_it_matters: Every reply shorter than the one before it still wasn't short enough.

prep.last_substantive_interaction: He sent me a numbered list of bathroom rules on June 15, asked me to confirm I agreed to them, and then filed my one-word reply for future reference.
three_talking_points: Ask whether the bathroom has been fine since June, or if there's something new.
If he brings up water again, ask whether he wants us to reduce faucet pressure or just keep using the mats.
If he's here about something else, let him say it first—he documents everything and I don't want to create a record of a problem that doesn't exist.

stories.title: The radio fund and the headcount
stories.moment: Wendy sent the question about the radio gift on May 5th: Rahul needed an answer by Friday, $135, "just say yes or no." I wrote back six days later saying I'd seen it just now. She asked for a headcount in the same message. I never gave her one. On June 2nd she wrote that she never got the Venmo, "not chasing you for it," but Rahul was going to think she forgot to ask. The real request was buried at the end: could I come the Friday before to help with the cake, the chairs, and the tent. I said I'd look at my calendar that week. I did not look at my calendar that week.
stories.why_it_matters: The answer that matters keeps getting deferred while smaller confirmations arrive late.

stories.title: Twenty days and a place setting
stories.moment: I told Wendy on June 5th that I would check my calendar and get back to her about setup day. She wrote again on June 24th. The gap is nineteen days. She opened with "I know you're busy" and said she wasn't saying it in a pointed way, she actually did know. Then: the tent people needed a final count by Monday. The last line was a question with no punctuation around it, just sitting there by itself. "I'd just like to know if I should set a place for you." Not whether I could come early, whether I was coming at all. The thread ends there.
stories.why_it_matters: The question narrows each time it goes unanswered, from help to attendance to a chair.

stories.title: billing is a trapdoor
stories.moment: I asked whether to build billing, since two clinics had asked for it and Dane thought it would close the seed round. Theo read the roadmap and sent back one line: "That's a features list, not a product." He pointed out that two of our three customers weren't using the thing we'd already built, and asked why nobody had checked. I wrote back defending myself—I did know why they weren't using it, one hadn't migrated their paper records and the other had a front desk manager retiring in four months. He replied the next day with six words: "Fair enough. Good luck with it." Three weeks later I cut billing from the roadmap entirely. The front desk manager was a product problem after all. I'd built for her replacement without noticing I was making that choice.
stories.why_it_matters: The concession arrived by email, never on the call where the argument happened.

stories.title: the twenty implementations rule
stories.moment: I sent Theo the services question—whether to take implementation work even though every vertical software company that does eventually can't stop. I argued that if twenty implementations produced a product that installs itself, the replacement revenue wasn't a bet but the output of what we'd just spent a year doing. The rule would hold because by the time we got to twenty we wouldn't want the work anymore. He wrote back: "That's a better argument than the one I was expecting." Then he told me to write the number down somewhere Dane could see it, because "rules you keep in your own head aren't rules." I never said the number twenty out loud to anyone before that thread.
stories.why_it_matters: Every argument here ends with me conceding, three weeks late, or him conceding immediately.

prep.last_substantive_interaction: I argued that capping services at twenty implementations was defensible if the work taught us to build a self-installing product. He said to write the number down where Dane could see it.

stories.title: per-seat is fear written down
stories.moment: Josiah sent pricing feedback I didn't ask for. He said per-seat was fighting the product, because clinics have eleven people touching the schedule and two generating revenue, so they'd share a login to avoid the cost. I wrote back at 11pm and admitted we went per-seat "because it was the thing I understood how to build, which is a bad reason that I have been calling a pricing strategy for four months." He'd caught something true. One of the FAQ lines was just fear written down, and I told him it was going. He made an intro the next morning.
stories.why_it_matters: The admission arrived twelve hours after the critique, which is fast for a founder to concede on pricing.

stories.title: domain hire plateaued at ten weeks
stories.moment: I asked Josiah how much he cared about domain background when he hired his first engineer. The candidate I wanted had never worked in healthcare. The two who had were both fine and neither was her. He said he cared a lot and was wrong. The domain hire was faster for ten weeks, then plateaued, "because he knew how the industry did things and kept building that." The one who didn't know anything asked why four times a day, and two of those questions were good. One changed the product. Then he reframed my question entirely: "Do you have the hours to be her domain for two months?" I didn't have the hours. I said I'd rather find them for the right person than not need them for the wrong one, and asked him to check whether that held up in June.
stories.why_it_matters: The question I thought I was asking turned out not to be the question that mattered.

stories.title: three weeks, two follow-ups, no intro
stories.moment: Josiah asked for an intro to Marguerite Vance, who led my round and kept coming up as someone who understood the operator side of what he was building. I said yes immediately and asked for a few days to think about framing. Twenty-seven days later he followed up with no pressure, offering to draft something I could edit. Twenty-one days after that he wrote again: "Last time I'll bring this up, promise." He said if I'd landed on no, he'd rather know than keep wondering whether his email went to spam. I never sent the intro. He closed the loop himself by saying the scheduling demo from April looked really good.
stories.why_it_matters: The gap between saying yes and going silent lasted seven weeks, which is long enough to be a decision.

stories.title: the room that was two rooms
stories.moment: Beatriz set up five exam rooms after I walked her through the system on Thursday. Then she sent a follow-up the same day: Exam 2 and Exam 3 were actually one room with a curtain down the middle. They tracked them separately because they could double-book for exams, but if one side had surgery prep they had to block both. She flagged it "before someone books a neuter on one side and a puppy wellness check on the other." I thanked her five days later and admitted I had no idea how to model it without wrecking the interface.
stories.why_it_matters: The physical layout broke an assumption the software was built on.

stories.title: she sent it the same day
stories.moment: Beatriz confirmed our 11am meeting that morning. By the time she sent the curtain-room problem, we'd already done the walkthrough, entered all five rooms, and I'd left. She could have waited until it caused an actual scheduling collision or mentioned it the next time I came by. Instead she wrote it up the same afternoon, while the setup was still fresh and before anyone had tried to use the system in anger.
stories.why_it_matters: The correction arrived before the mistake could compound.
